095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thi: Downton Abbey is the hugely popular British TV drama (2010-2015) about the Earl of Grantham's family and their servants in the early twentieth century, following the manor through war, scandal, and the slow erosion of the aristocracy. Its strict class order turns out to be fertile ground for philosophy: the meaning of work, whether manners are morality, when lying is justified, women's rights, disability, and whether a life like Carson's or a death like Sybil's can be made sense of at all.
096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - T: Hannibal Lecter is the cultured psychiatrist and cannibal serial killer at the center of Thomas Harris's novels, five films including The Silence of the Lambs, and the TV series Hannibal. He fascinates because he is brilliant, polite, and monstrous at once, which raises uncomfortable questions: what exactly is wrong with eating people, can his killings be dressed up in ethical theories, why do we admire an aesthete of murder, and what does his empathy with Will Graham and Clarice Starling say about us.
097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Phil: The Walking Dead is the long-running AMC series (and comic) about survivors of a zombie apocalypse where everyone is already infected. With civilization gone, it becomes a pressure test for ethics: why be moral when survival pushes against it, whether Dale's Kantian principles or Shane's consequentialism fit the new world, how attempted communities like Woodbury and Terminus fail, whether Jenner's despair was right, and what Carol's transformations cost.
098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy: The Princess Bride is the beloved 1987 fairy-tale adventure film, drawn from William Goldman's novel, about the farmhand Westley, the princess Buttercup, the avenger Inigo, and a giant named Fezzik, complete with a Battle of Wits and Miracle Max. Beneath the jokes sits real philosophy: what makes a promise binding, whether men of action may lie, why revenge feels sweet, what 'inconceivable' actually means, and whether Westley's rhetoric or Vizzini's logic wins the day.
099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Do: Louis C.K. is the American stand-up comedian whose specials and the FX series Louie turned confession into comedy, mining parenthood, boredom, sex, and mortality. His bits read like thought experiments: why everything's amazing and nobody's happy, whether you get to be bored, what the 'forever empty' of death does to us, when anger beats hatred, and whether Dr. Bigelow's advice about back pain and heartbreak is really Stoicism wearing a cardigan.
100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy -: Batman and Superman are DC Comics' two oldest and most famous superheroes: the billionaire vigilante who strikes fear into Gotham's criminals and the invulnerable Kryptonian who stands for truth and hope. Pitting them against each other is really an argument about ideals - who should we try to be like? Their rivalry raises questions of philosophical anarchism, chivalric self-restraint, Nietzsche's overman, evolutionary fitness, and whether a god is what we actually need.
101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality: Discworld is Terry Pratchett's comic fantasy series of forty-one novels set on a flat world carried through space by four elephants and a turtle. The jokes carry surprising philosophical weight: golems as metaphors for the words society writes into our heads, a con artist running the post office, Lord Vetinari's friendly guide to tyranny, censorship in a city's first newspaper, witches and dwarfs negotiating identity, and what Sam Vimes's stubborn commonsense can teach professional philosophy.
102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Gran: Orphan Black is the BBC America thriller (2013-2017) in which con artist Sarah Manning discovers she is one of many clones - all played by Tatiana Maslany - monitored by a biotech corporation that owns their DNA. The premise drives hard questions: can a company legally or morally own people, what makes each clone a distinct self, are the clones harmed by being engineered to exist, what do Buddhist ideas and sisterhood offer them, and is Sarah responsible for what her makers built into her.
103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel: David Bowie was the English singer-songwriter (1947-2016) who reinvented himself across five decades, from Ziggy Stardust and the Thin White Duke to the late-career Blackstar, shaping glam rock, electronic music, and popular culture. The constant change was itself his philosophy: Sartrean self-creation, whether anything persists beneath the personas, the artifice of authenticity, Buddhist impermanence, deliberate nonsense in his lyrics, and what it means to make facing death into a final work of art.
104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break: Red Rising is Pierce Brown's science fiction series (beginning 2015) about Darrow, a miner bred for a color-coded caste system on Mars, who is surgically remade as a member of the ruling Gold elite to destroy the society from within. Its brutal world is a playground for big questions: social Darwinism masquerading as nature, what makes a person the same after total transformation, whether Darrow is a hero or just a subtler villain, and whether love or vengeance should fuel a revolution.
